documents.unit: CUNY Board of Trustees (system policy applying to the Graduate Center)
documents.title: CUNY Academic Integrity Policy (2024)
documents.summary: CUNY's system-wide academic integrity policy, revised in 2024 to cover AI. It classes unauthorized AI use and uncited AI content as cheating or plagiarism and requires AI use to follow assignment-level rules set by the instructor, while the explanation frames AI skills as part of CUNY's mission.
documents.stance_why: The policy bans AI generation of assignments or exams 'without written authorization from the instructor' but also says 'Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor.' It sets no uniform stance and hands the decision to instructors, with no tiers, so delegates.

units.why: Opening sentence names sanctions for academic dishonesty ('failing or otherwise reduced grades... suspension or expulsion'), the framework that later AI definitions plug into. P37 fits because penalties are stated in advance; it is not AI-specific but governs AI cheating too.
units.anchor: Penalties for academic dishonesty include academic sanctions, such as failing or otherwise reduced grades

units.why: Defines cheating to include 'unauthorized use... of... artificial intelligence (AI) systems' during an academic exercise. This classifies unauthorized AI use as cheating, so P36 (misconduct) rather than P61, which is about defining AI itself.
units.anchor: unauthorized use or attempted use of material, information, notes, study aids, devices, artificial intelligence (AI)
units.frag_end: or communication during an academic exercise
units.policy: Unauthorized use or attempted use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems during an academic exercise is cheating

units.why: Lists copying from a generative AI system as cheating: 'Copying from another person or from a generative AI system'. It forbids submitting AI-copied work for credit, so P19 fits best; P36 is the framing but the content is the ban on submitting AI-produced work.
units.anchor: Copying from another person or from a generative AI system
units.frag_end: work submitted for credit or a grade

units.why: Bars uploading work or assignments to third-party platforms 'beyond those assigned for the class' without authorization. This restricts sending assignments or exams to outside platforms, matching P20 rather than P49 because it concerns assignments and work, not only course materials.
units.anchor: uploading work or submitting class assignments or exams to third party platforms and websites beyond

units.why: States generative AI use must follow assignment-level policy: 'must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments'. The system sets no uniform rule and defers to the course, so P04.
units.anchor: Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for

units.why: The same sentence says the policy is 'defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor', so expectations are set at course level. P09 fits (AI expectations in the syllabus or instructions), though 'and/or communicated' makes it softer than a mandate.
units.anchor: as defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor
units.policy: Instructors define the AI usage policy for specific assignments in the course syllabus and/or communicate it

units.why: Prohibits using AI to generate content for assignments or exams 'without written authorization from the instructor'. Banned unless explicitly authorized, so restrict. I chose P06 (fallback: no AI unless authorized) because the defining feature is the authorization default; P19 is the content ban but lacks the authorization condition.
units.anchor: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate content for assignments or exams
units.frag_end: without written authorization from the instructor

units.why: Names 'language models or code generators' within the unauthorized-generation example, extending the rule to code tools. It is an explicit coverage statement for code generators, not built-in IDE tools, so P19 not P07.
units.anchor: including but not limited to language models or code generators
units.frag_end: without written authorization from the instructor
units.policy: Using language models or code generators to generate content for assignments or exams without written authorization from the instructor is cheating

units.why: Exam clause: unauthorized electronic devices during an examination 'to copy, retrieve, generate or send information'. 'Generate' covers AI generation on exams; P22 fits.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices

units.why: Defines cheating as submitting content generated by an AI tool 'as solely your own work'. This is a rule that submitted work must be the student's own, so P29; the misconduct classification is secondary.

units.why: The same clause ends with content 'generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation' being cheating. It ties acceptable use to citation, so P24; it also covers paraphrasing tools.
units.anchor: content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation

units.why: Plagiarism example: copying an AI tool's words or images without quotation marks and citations. It requires quotation and citation of AI output; P24 covers citing AI use.

units.why: Plagiarism example: use of AI-generated content 'even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source'. I code the citation duty here (P24); the unauthorized-use ban is coded elsewhere. This unit stresses that paraphrasing does not remove the duty to cite.
units.anchor: use of AI-generated content, whether in whole or in part, even when paraphrased, without citing
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source

units.why: The plagiarism list includes 'Unauthorized use of AI-generated content', classing it as plagiarism. This is the misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content is plagiarism

units.why: Policy says the link to the integrity policy should be in the LMS shell and 'recommended' in each syllabus. It communicates expectations though not AI-specific; P09 is nearest, and 'recommended' gives modality should.

units.why: Requires orientations for new faculty and students to include academic integrity, which now covers AI. It is communicating expectations; P09 is the nearest type, and P63 (faculty learning about AI) does not fit because AI is not named.

units.why: Opening rationale: cheating confers 'an unfair advantage over others, which undermines educational equity and fairness'. It explains why integrity rules exist and is not about AI or skill-building, so P41 does not fit; UNCOVERED.

units.why: Colleges may adopt more specific procedures but they 'must be consistent with the policy'. It sets how the system policy relates to college rules; framework, P56.

notes: Only the CUNY system Academic Integrity Policy was available; the Graduate Center's own draft AI guidelines were inaccessible. Several units (P37, P64, P40) are general integrity procedures that cover AI misuse without naming AI.
